source: Edwards and Schuster (2026) Ask or Assume? Uncertainty-Aware Clarification-Seeking in Coding Agents
finding: On underspecified SWE-bench Verified (gap 1), a scaffold with a separate intent-checker that decides when to ask matched the forced-ask baseline and the fully specified task. One agent told to check itself did worse.
numbers: N=500 tasks, Claude Sonnet 4.5: FULL 70.8, HIDDEN (never ask) 54.8, INTERACTIVE (forced ask) 70.4, UA-SINGLE 61.2, UA-MULTI 69.4 (vs UA-SINGLE p<0.001; vs FULL p=0.458). Tasks where agent queried: UA-MULTI 344, UA-SINGLE 369, forced baseline 496. Resolve rate when UA-MULTI did not ask: 76.92 (FULL 77.56). Kimi K2.6: FULL 72.8, HIDDEN 55.4, INTERACTIVE 47.2, UA-SINGLE 61.6, UA-MULTI 69.4, but 8.71 queries per task (poor calibration).
quote: decouples underspecification detection from code execution
limits: Two backbones, one benchmark, simulated oracle user. No equal-token comparison: UA-MULTI uses a second agent and 3.06 questions per task vs 1.02 for forced-ask. Forced-ask failed on Kimi from instruction-following errors, so it is not a clean always-ask arm.
agent_relevance: Supports a gated clarify step. A separate cheap ambiguity check beat self-checking inside the same agent. Gap 1 partly closed: gate beats never-ask and ties forced-ask on quality; token parity still untested.

source: Vijayvargiya et al. (2026) Ambig-SWE: Interactive Agents to Overcome Underspecificity in Software Engineering (ICLR 2026)
finding: Models default to not asking and cannot tell well-specified from underspecified tasks. Once they do get answers, they gain a lot.
numbers: Interaction raises resolve rate on underspecified inputs by up to 74% over non-interactive. Detection accuracy 89% (Claude Sonnet 4) and 84% (Claude Sonnet 3.5) were the only good ones; some models at chance (50%); one model 100% false-negative (never interacts). Prompt encouragement changes behaviour unevenly (Deepseek-v2 got worse with stronger encouragement).
limits: Software-engineering tasks only; simulated user; the interaction condition makes asking compulsory, so it is not a test of a gate. Efficiency (steps) did not improve.
agent_relevance: Detection of ambiguity is the weak link, not the ability to use answers. Argues for an explicit detect-then-ask slot and for testing the detector alone.

source: Suri et al. (2026) Structured Uncertainty guided Clarification for LLM Agents (SAGE-Agent, ClarifyBench)
finding: Choosing which question to ask by expected value of information over tool parameters beats prompting, and its signal can be used for RL.
numbers: 39% higher coverage on ambiguous tasks than strong prompting and uncertainty baselines; When2Call accuracy 36.5 to 65.2 (3B) and 36.7 to 62.9 (7B) after uncertainty-weighted GRPO training.
limits: Abstract and PDF text skimmed; tool-calling tasks, not open reasoning. Part of the gain comes from training.
agent_relevance: A principled ask/do-not-ask rule (value of information against question cost) is a candidate gate design; the EVPI part can be used at inference without training.

source: Shaikh et al. (2025) Navigating Rifts in Human-LLM Grounding: Study and Benchmark
finding: Gaps 2 and 8. Newer chat and reasoning models still do not initiate grounding on real user logs. A simple gated prompt fixes much of it.
numbers: From WildChat, MultiWOZ, Bing Chat logs: LLMs 3x less likely to initiate clarification and 16x less likely to give follow-up requests than humans. RIFTS test: GPT-4o 25.26, 4o-mini 24.48, o3-mini 25.26, Claude Sonnet 3.5 26.95, Opus 3 24.57, Llama 3.1 8B 24.22, 70B 23.88 (all below the 33% random level; average 23.23). No-grounding-needed items 96.09% correct; other categories 2.22% correct initiative. Llama 3.1 8B + GROUND (a forecaster decides when to add a clarify or follow-up prompt) 54.48 (+/-2.45), better than all others by at least 32 points.
quote: o3-mini regularly begins reasoning without verifying grounding
limits: Models are 2024-era (o3-mini is the only reasoning model); no 2026 frontier models. Benchmark is built from cases where GPT models failed, so absolute scores are biased low. The intervention uses a trained forecaster, not a pure prompt.
agent_relevance: Reasoning models do not fix it: o3-mini begins reasoning without checking grounding. Timing, not frequency, was repaired by a gate that decides when to add the clarify prompt.

source: Laban et al. (2025) LLMs Get Lost In Multi-Turn Conversation (reasoning models, recap, temperature)
finding: Gaps 2 and 4. Reasoning models degrade like the rest. Recap helps only partly; temperature 0 does not fix sharded unreliability.
numbers: 15 LLMs incl. o3, Deepseek-R1, Gemini 2.5 Pro, Claude 3.7 Sonnet, GPT-4.1; reasoning models deteriorate similarly; their responses are 33% longer, with more assumptions. Table 2 (4 tasks): GPT-4o-mini Full 86.8, Concat 84.4, Sharded 50.4, Recap 66.5, Snowball 61.8; GPT-4o 93.0, 90.9, 59.1, 76.6, 65.3. Snowball mitigates 15-20% of the Full-to-Sharded drop. Temperature: GPT-4o-mini sharded unreliability does not fall as assistant temp goes 1.0 to 0.0 (49.8, 46.8, 51.0 in one row).
quote: reasoning models ... deteriorate in similar ways to non-reasoning models
limits: Recap on the last turn needs knowing it is the last turn, so the authors call it unrealistic. Recap and snowball add tokens and were not compared at equal tokens. Tested only on GPT-4o and 4o-mini. Column order of Table 2 read from PDF text.
agent_relevance: Restating accumulated requirements helps but does not close the gap (GPT-4o recap recovers 17.5 of 33.9 lost points, about 52%; snowball about 18%). Thinking longer is not a substitute for asking or restating.

source: Li et al. (2023, v3 2024) Theory of Mind for Multi-Agent Collaboration via Large Language Models
finding: Gap 3. The round counts 28.3 vs 12.3 cannot be tied to belief vs no belief for GPT-4. Table row labels are lost in text extraction and the prose is inconsistent. Treat the round-count gain as unproven; the clear belief gains are ToM probe accuracy and fewer invalid actions.
numbers: Table 1 values (rows partly unlabeled in PDF text): ChatGPT score 43+/-4.7, 30.0 rounds, 62.5% valid; a second row 90, 28.3+/-2.6 rounds, 71.8% valid; GPT-4 90, 12.3+/-2.0, 86.1%; next row 90, 11.0; CBS planner 6.0; MAPPO 11.0 per prose. Prose: with explicit belief representations being more efficient (28.3 vs. 12.3 rounds). Table 2 ToM: GPT-4+Belief introspection 97.2%, 1st-order 80.1%, 2nd-order 69.4%. Three teammates, three trials, temperature 0.
limits: Three agents in one text bomb game, three trials: tiny N. The table image could not be rendered (no pdftoppm), so the row-to-label mapping of 28.3 is inferred. Most likely 28.3 is a ChatGPT-with-belief row, unverified. For GPT-4 the likeliest reading is 12.3 to 11.0.
agent_relevance: Do not cite 28.3. Belief text mainly cuts invalid actions and raises ToM probe accuracy; the speed gain for GPT-4 is small (12.3 to 11.0) and untested for significance.

source: Clark and Wilkes-Gibbs (1986) Referring as a collaborative process, Cognition 22
finding: Gap 5. Pairs of strangers arranging 12 tangram figures got faster and used fewer turns across six trials, as the collaborative model predicts.
numbers: Exp 1: 8 pairs x 12 figures x 6 trials (576 figure placements, 9,792 words transcribed), error rate 2%. Director words per figure fell from 41 in trial 1 to 8 in trial 6, F(1,35)=44.31, p<.001. Director turns per figure 3.7 to about 1, F(1,35)=79.59, p<.001. Hardest figure averaged 26.5 words per trial (39.6 on trial 1), easiest 9.7 (24).
limits: Small sample (8 pairs), students, one task. Later work attributes part of the shortening to alignment through repetition rather than partner-specific grounding (not opened here).
agent_relevance: Human baseline for how the cost of grounding falls with shared history: about 5x fewer words by trial 6. A scaffold that restates settled terms once and then reuses them is a human-like pattern.

source: Brennan and Clark (1996) Conceptual pacts and lexical choice in conversation, JEP:LMC 22
finding: Gap 5. Speakers keep partner-specific terms (conceptual pacts) and drop them more often when the partner changes.
numbers: Same vs new matcher: directors reused the last-B-trial term in trial C1 48% with the same matcher vs 18% after switching, F1(1,18)=5.18, p<.05 (by items p=.08). After a firm pact over four B trials directors kept an over-informative term (e.g. pennyloafer) 46% of the time in the first C trial (38% by verbatim criterion); 61% vs 31% retained after four vs one B trial. Hedges fell from 26% to 2% as pacts formed. Different pairs agreed on basic-level terms only about 10%, inside the 7-18% range of Furnas et al. 1987. Card placement errors about 2%.
limits: Student pairs, card matching, four target objects; the same-vs-new-partner effect was only marginal by items. Which experiment each participant count (72 and 50 appear in the text) belongs to was not verified.
agent_relevance: Terms are agreed with a particular partner, not just remembered. Writing partner-specific labels into a visible ledger, and flagging that they may not hold for a new reader, matches the finding.

source: Metzing and Brennan (2003) When conceptual pacts are broken (replication record, background knowledge only)
finding: Recalled from background knowledge, not verified this session: a new partner using an old term cost comprehension time in eye-tracking.
limits: Numbers not seen. The replication record for conceptual pacts remains unchecked, so the replication half of gap 5 stays open.

source: Kim et al. (2026) Towards a Science of Scaling Agent Systems (error amplification detail)
finding: Gap 10. Trace-level error amplification is a ratio to a single agent defined as 1.0, so the paper does not test a single agent with an internal verifier. After controls, error amplification itself did not predict performance.
numbers: Trace-level amplification: single agent 1.0, centralized 4.4, decentralized 7.8, hybrid 5.1, independent 17.2. Regression: error amplification coefficient 0.014, p=0.658 after controls. Task-level amplification for verifying architectures about 1.1 to 1.3 (text partly cut). SWE-bench Verified: all multi-agent forms slightly worse than single agent.
limits: 17.2 vs 4.4 is descriptive and mixes architecture with cost; the non-significant coefficient weakens a causal reading. No self-verifier arm was run.
agent_relevance: Gap 10 stays open: nothing here shows whether an internal verifier cuts single-agent error. Do not use 17.2 vs 4.4 as support for a single-agent verifier.

source: Hernandez and Wilson (2026) PARLEY: Evaluating LLM Collaboration Through Cooperative Asymmetric Puzzles
finding: Gaps 7 and 9. GPT-4o pairs on four psychology-based tasks fail in ways unlike human breakdowns. A failure-taxonomy prompt raised success by 10 points.
numbers: N=400 conversations (100 per task), success 60.5%; Tangram referential task 34.0%, Scene Comparison 80.0%. Six failure types; grounding failures 17.4% of instances (42.6% in Scene Comparison, 40.4% in Tangram). Intervention N=200: success 60.5 to 70.5 (+10.0 pp, p=.019 Fisher); Tangram 34 to 46, Map Task 55 to 68, Scene 80 to 88, Grid 73 to 80.
quote: where humans show egocentric bias, agents show excessive compliance
limits: One model (GPT-4o), LLM-as-judge taxonomy, 50 runs per task in the intervention, no multiple-comparison correction. A longer prompt could work by length alone.
agent_relevance: Gap 9: authors say where humans show egocentric bias, agents show excessive compliance, and where humans adapt, agents repeat failed strategies. No human-like egocentric reference error seen. A prompt naming failure modes helped moderately, a cheap checklist for the schema.

source: Anon. (2026) Aligned but Not Partner-Specific: How Multimodal LLM Agents Succeed in Reference Games Without Forming Conceptual Pacts
finding: Gaps 5 and 9. Direct LLM test of conceptual pacts against human dyads on KTH Tangrams. Agents do not shorten; their label overlap is the same for real and shuffled pseudo-dyads.
numbers: Humans compress descriptions across rounds and raise label overlap with partners; agents keep fixed effort, verbose from round one; near-ceiling label overlap statistically indistinguishable between real and pseudo dyads. Test statistics not recorded (abstract only).
limits: Abstract page only; numbers not seen.
agent_relevance: LLMs coordinate without partner-specific pacts. For a single agent, shared terms will not form on their own; they must be written down.

source: Hua et al. (2024) Talk Less, Interact Better: Evaluating In-context Conversational Adaptation in Multimodal LLMs (ICCA)
finding: Gaps 5 and 9. MLLMs understand a partner's increasingly short language but do not shorten their own. Heavy prompting makes some (GPT-4) do it.
numbers: No numbers recorded (abstract only): no spontaneous efficiency gain over rounds; elicited only in some models with heavy-handed prompting.
agent_relevance: Consistent with d12: entrainment is not learned in-context by default.

source: Anon. (2026) A Benchmark to Assess Common Ground in Human-AI Collaboration
finding: Gaps 6 and 9. A puzzle benchmark with a human study reproduces human-human common-ground findings and shows clear human-AI divergences.
numbers: No effect sizes recorded (abstract and text skim only).
limits: Does not test Klein et al. Basic Compact items (predictability, directability) by name.
agent_relevance: Candidate harness for a grounding test of our agent; numbers not available.

source: Anon. (2026) Knowing the User Is Not Knowing What We Established: Grounding Awareness in Personal Agents (Grounding Layer)
finding: Gaps 3 and 8. A single agent that explicitly tracks the status of each proposal (accepted, unacknowledged, revised, scoped) acts far more correctly. More user information can raise execution of unacknowledged proposals.
numbers: Sensitivity with raw history rises from 0.06 to 0.56 (DeepSeek) and 0.13 to 0.49 (Qwen) with the training-free Grounding Layer; LangMem 0.17 to 0.36 and 0.21 to 0.51. With Mem0, retaining more information raised Contextual Selectivity 0.26 to 0.53 and MemOS 0.34 to 0.46. With full history, 71% of errors occur at action selection although status information is available.
limits: Controlled synthetic benchmark; open models plus GPT-5-mini as scorer. Sensitivity is the authors' own measure. Some pairings of numbers to conditions read from PDF text.
agent_relevance: Closest direct test of an explicit shared-understanding slot inside one agent. A written status per agreement beats memory alone, which supports gap 3: the slot helps single agents, not only games.

source: Anon. (2026) When to Ask, When to Answer: Strategic Clarification for Ambiguous Reference Resolution in Dialogue (BACE)
finding: Gaps 1 and 8. LLMs are biased toward premature answering. A small belief-tracking chooser on a frozen model picks the right number of questions better than GRPO and ArCHer.
numbers: On SIMMC 2.1 reference tasks: BACE reward about 0.93 to 0.95 in the tables read; SFT within 0.002 of BACE in reward in Table 3; one policy asks on 98.5% of episodes that need no question; Ask F1 0.245 for a comparator vs BACE 0.931. Number-to-method mapping partly uncertain from PDF text.
limits: Numbers partly read from garbled text; single dataset; trains a 27.7M-parameter chooser. Not an equal-token prompt-only test.
agent_relevance: Over-asking and under-asking both occur, so a gate needs a stop rule (value of the next question).

source: Anon. (2026) Is That Clear? The Impacts of Clarifying Questions on Human-LLM Interaction
finding: Gap 1 boundary condition. Clarifying questions raise perceived understanding but make users scrutinise answers less and accept wrong ones more.
numbers: Controlled experiment N=180, six decision scenarios. CQs increased perceived understanding and satisfaction; less review time; more unchanged acceptance including erroneous answers; violations in CQ-adjacent sub-decisions accepted more often. No effect sizes recorded (abstract).
agent_relevance: A clarify step can create false trust: the agent should not treat having asked as proof of alignment (links to over-prediction of shared understanding, K18).

source: Anon. (2026) When AI Agents Act on Our Behalf: A Taxonomy of Human-Agent Interaction Failure; and Babysitting AI Agents (MANDATE)
finding: Gap 6. Field-incident studies of agent failures. They map onto predictability and directability problems but do not test them.
numbers: 695 incidents coded into 12 failure modes (all at both low and high autonomy). MANDATE: 163,487 Reddit posts, 23 failure categories in 7 groups; follow-up N=73 users: failures rated more severe are rated harder to notice (arXiv 2610.34748).
limits: Incident reports are self-selected; neither tests Klein et al. requirements by name; abstracts only.
agent_relevance: Gap 6 stays mostly open: the closest evidence is descriptive. Controls between full delegation and manual work are called for.

source: Beyond Division of Labor: How Roles Shape Feedback and Recovery in Multi-Agent Systems (2026) and Signed but Not Safe (2026), both citing MAST
finding: Gap 7. Two later papers touch MAST ideas. Role prompts mattered through when the reviewer lets the team submit, not through specialisation. No paper found that re-runs the +9.4% ChatDev role fix.
numbers: Beyond Division of Labor: three open models on Omni-MATH and SciBench; removing roles did not lower first-pass accuracy; forcing submission each cycle raised recovery from 0.198 to 0.613 (400 Omni-MATH problems, gemma-4); role-free minus role-structured recovery at equal verdicts +0.009, 95% interval [-0.014, +0.033]. Signed but Not Safe (2611.07483): 1,440 trajectories on Qwen3-8B, signed manifests cut unsafe commits under attack from 69.4% to 9.0% (comparison arm per abstract, not verified).
limits: Semantic Scholar listed 89 papers citing Shaikh 2024 and many citing MAST; only titles and abstracts of a handful opened. Neither paper replicates the ChatDev +9.4%.
agent_relevance: Role effects can be a submission-gate effect, not a specialisation effect. Handoff requirement integrity (explicit checkable requirement lists) has a single-agent analogue.
